item.title: Spark Program | SkillPass Care — Transferable Warranty Pilot for Second-Hand Products on CKB
item.dc:creator: Dangbaty2004
item.description:
Applicant: Dang Ba Ty (@Dangbaty2004)
GitHub: tydeptrai21042004
Discord: tyforwork
Email: dangbaty.work@gmail.com
Funding requested: $500 USD, payable in equivalent CKB
Estimated duration: 4 weeks
Project category: CKB dApp / Product MVP / Early User Validation
Target network: CKB Pudge Testnet

Project links:

  • SkillPass protocol: GitHub - tydeptrai21042004/ckb-skill · GitHub

  • SkillPass Care application: GitHub - tydeptrai21042004/SkillPass-Care · GitHub

  • SkillPass demo: https://ckb-skill.vercel.app/

  • SkillPass Care demo: https://skill-pass-care-api.vercel.app/

  • CKBuilder technical review: SkillPass: portable service rights on CKB with SkillPass Care as a second-hand product coverage reference app · Issue #37 · Nervos-Community-Catalyst/CKBuilder-projects · GitHub

  • Existing real Testnet evidence: Real CKB Testnet — Deploy + Lifecycle · tydeptrai21042004/ckb-skill@e4eb356 · GitHub

1. Project Overview

SkillPass Care is a CKB-based application for transferable product-service coverage, initially focusing on refurbished and second-hand electronic devices.

The problem is straightforward: when a product is resold, any remaining warranty or service entitlement may be difficult for the next owner to verify or use, particularly if different service providers maintain separate customer records.

SkillPass Care explores a different approach. A service entitlement is represented by a transferable Capability Cell on CKB, while the application maintains the coverage plan, remaining service units, and service history.

When Alice transfers the entitlement to Bob, authorized providers can verify Bob’s current ownership from CKB without relying on a shared entitlement-owner database.

An existing SkillPass Testnet experiment has already demonstrated issuance, transfer, and ownership verification. The proposed Spark project will turn this technical foundation into a usable warranty pilot and test whether the workflow provides practical value to users and service providers.

The objective is to deliver and evaluate one complete product-service lifecycle, not to develop a new general-purpose protocol.

The funded work will focus on a limited warranty workflow, real Testnet ownership integration, user-facing improvements, and initial external validation.

2. Team Profile

I am Dang Ba Ty, an independent developer contributing to the Nervos CKB ecosystem.

My work has focused on CKB Cell-based applications, transaction construction, verification, and developer-facing tools.

I developed the underlying SkillPass protocol and the SkillPass Care reference application. Both are publicly available, with ongoing technical discussion through the CKBuilder program.

SkillPass has received CKBuilder mentorship support, including the assignment of @zhangsoledad for technical review.

Relevant development experience includes:

  • Rust and ckb-std for CKB Type Scripts.

  • TypeScript, Node.js, and React for applications and verification tooling.

  • CCC and wallet integration for CKB transactions.

  • PostgreSQL for persistent application state.

  • GitHub Actions for reproducible testing and public technical evidence.

I will be responsible for implementation, Testnet validation, documentation, user-testing coordination, and reporting.

External reviewers and pilot participants will be invited to evaluate the results; their participation is not assumed or presented as confirmed.

3. Project Background

Consider a customer who purchases a refurbished smartphone with three remaining service units.

The customer, Alice, uses one diagnostic service at Provider A. She then sells the phone to Bob.

Bob wants to use the two remaining service units at Provider B.

In a conventional provider-specific warranty system, this process may require manual ownership updates, account migration, or coordination between providers. A warranty recorded only against Alice’s original customer account may not automatically follow a transferable entitlement.

SkillPass Care investigates whether CKB can provide a shared ownership reference without requiring each provider to maintain synchronized ownership records.

The proposed workflow is:

  1. Alice receives a service entitlement containing three coverage units.

  2. Provider A verifies Alice and records one service, leaving two units.

  3. Alice transfers the Capability Cell to Bob through a CKB transaction.

  4. After the transfer is confirmed, Alice is no longer authorized to use the entitlement.

  5. Provider B independently verifies Bob and processes another service.

  6. The remaining balance becomes one unit, with both service events preserved.

This scenario provides a concrete way to test the usefulness of portable service rights.

The project does not assume that customers or businesses already demand blockchain-based warranties. Establishing whether the workflow is understandable, useful, and preferable to simpler alternatives is part of the proposed validation.

4. Proposed Solution

SkillPass Care will provide a small, end-to-end warranty application covering issuance, service usage, ownership transfer, and continued service eligibility.

The pilot will use one representative refurbished-electronics coverage plan, with a fixed service-unit allowance and two provider configurations.

4.1 Customer experience

A customer will be able to:

  • View an assigned service entitlement and its remaining coverage.

  • Connect a supported CKB wallet to verify entitlement ownership.

  • Transfer the entitlement to another wallet.

  • Review service history and remaining service units.

  • Present the entitlement to a provider for verification.

The application will explain the difference between pending, confirmed, rejected, and unavailable verification results.

4.2 Provider experience

A participating provider will be able to:

  • Check the current entitlement holder against CKB.

  • Review the applicable coverage plan and remaining service units.

  • Record a permitted service event.

  • Reject requests from the previous owner after a confirmed transfer.

  • Detect duplicate service submissions and prevent repeated consumption.

Provider verification will use the current live Capability Cell and the application’s coverage rules.

4.3 Pilot scope

The initial pilot will focus on one complete scenario rather than supporting an open-ended warranty marketplace.

The acceptance scenario is:

Step Expected result
Alice receives coverage 3 units
Provider A completes diagnostic 2 units
Alice transfers entitlement to Bob CKB ownership changes
Alice requests another service DENY
Bob requests service at Provider B ALLOW
Provider B completes service 1 unit
Service history is inspected Both provider events retained

The application will support English-language instructions and expose sufficient information for participants to understand the process without inspecting smart-contract code.

The pilot will not claim that ownership of a digital service entitlement independently proves ownership or possession of the associated physical device. Product identity and eligibility remain subject to issuer and provider verification.

5. Technical Approach

SkillPass Care uses two distinct layers.

5.1 CKB ownership layer

The existing SkillPass protocol represents a service entitlement through a Capability Cell.

The live Cell’s lock identifies the current authorized holder, while the Capability Type Script constrains entitlement transitions.

The application will use the existing canonical SkillPass verification interfaces to establish current ownership.

Provider decisions must account for:

  • The recognized Type Script deployment.

  • The current live Capability Cell.

  • The entitlement identity and applicable policy.

  • The claimant’s wallet authorization.

  • Transaction confirmation and chain-state freshness.

  • Unavailable or contradictory verification evidence.

An unavailable RPC response must not be interpreted as successful authorization.

5.2 Application layer

SkillPass Care maintains product-specific state separately from CKB ownership.

This includes the coverage plan, remaining service units, service-event history, provider authorization, and issuer suspension or revocation.

The existing implementation uses TypeScript, React, Node.js, and PostgreSQL.

The funded work will connect the application to the real SkillPass Testnet ownership path, improve the customer/provider workflow, and exercise the complete lifecycle through the hosted application.

The pilot will reuse the existing Capability contract, ownership interfaces, and Care domain model. It will not introduce another blockchain protocol or a replacement for CCC.

5.3 Service integrity

The pilot will test that:

  • A previous owner cannot consume coverage after a confirmed transfer.

  • The same service request cannot consume coverage twice.

  • Concurrent service requests cannot consume more units than remain available.

  • Provider authorization is bound to the specific entitlement and requested service.

  • Missing chain evidence leaves the operation unapproved.

  • Ownership transfer preserves the associated coverage history.

A configurable confirmation policy will be documented. No fixed confirmation depth will be presented as an absolute finality guarantee.

The project will remain on CKB Pudge Testnet. It is not intended to provide production-grade insurance, a legally enforceable warranty, or custody of real customer funds.

6. Execution Plan and Milestones

Total duration: 4 weeks

M1 — Real Testnet Ownership Integration

Week 1

Connect SkillPass Care to the existing canonical SkillPass ownership-verification path.

Tasks:

  • Pin the supported Capability deployment and protocol version.

  • Integrate real Testnet entitlement lookup and authorization.

  • Connect the Care runtime to canonical SkillPass ownership evidence.

  • Verify current-owner and previous-owner behavior.

  • Establish reproducible integration tests.

Deliverable: A working Care application that can distinguish valid, stale, and unavailable ownership using CKB Testnet evidence.

Acceptance criteria: The application verifies an existing real Capability ownership state and rejects unsupported or stale ownership rather than falling back to simulated authorization.

M2 — Transferable Warranty Product MVP

Week 2

Complete the user-facing warranty lifecycle.

Tasks:

  • Connect the existing coverage-plan workflow to real ownership verification.

  • Support the Alice-to-Bob wallet transfer scenario.

  • Preserve coverage units and service history across transfer.

  • Complete Provider A and Provider B service workflows.

  • Improve customer-facing transaction and authorization status reporting.

Deliverable: A public Testnet-oriented application demonstrating the full transfer-and-service workflow.

Acceptance criteria: The documented scenario produces 3 → 2 → transfer → 1 coverage units, with Alice rejected and Bob authorized after the confirmed transfer.

M3 — Reliability and Pilot Preparation

Week 3

Prepare the product for controlled external evaluation.

Tasks:

  • Test duplicate requests and concurrent service consumption.

  • Test stale ownership, incompatible entitlements, and temporary RPC failures.

  • Validate restart-safe Care records using PostgreSQL.

  • Run two separately configured provider instances or processes.

  • Prepare a short user guide and a repeatable pilot script.

Deliverable: A tested pilot release with documented failure scenarios and a guided walkthrough.

Acceptance criteria: Automated tests pass for the principal authorization, transfer, quota, and failure-handling scenarios. Any unresolved failure is documented rather than silently treated as success.

M4 — Early User Validation and Final Evidence

Week 4

Conduct an initial product evaluation and publish the results.

Tasks:

  • Invite potential refurbished-electronics sellers, repair providers, and individual users to test the workflow.

  • Target at least three external participant sessions, including feedback from at least one potential service provider.

  • Record whether participants can understand ownership transfer, remaining coverage, and service eligibility.

  • Collect usability concerns and assess whether simpler non-blockchain alternatives would meet their needs.

  • Publish the final Testnet evidence package, reproduction instructions, and summary report.

Deliverable: Public pilot report, reproducible technical evidence, and updated application documentation.

Acceptance criteria: Completed outreach and testing are reported with actual participation counts, observed issues, and findings. If the recruitment target is not reached, the report will document the shortfall and the evidence actually obtained.

No external provider participation is claimed before it occurs.

7. Required Funding and Funding Breakdown

Total requested: $500 USD equivalent in CKB.

The funding supports incremental development and early product validation over four weeks.

Work package Funding
Canonical CKB ownership integration and verification $175
Transferable warranty MVP and provider workflows $150
External pilot preparation and user testing $100
Reproducible evidence, documentation, and final report $75
Total $500

The requested amount is intended to cover a limited validation phase, not the complete historical development cost of SkillPass or SkillPass Care.

Existing contract code, earlier Testnet transactions, application components, and prior testing will be reused without requesting retrospective funding.

The project will use public Testnet infrastructure and existing open-source tooling wherever feasible.

I will publish milestone updates and a final summary of fund allocation and completed work.

8. Deliverables and How to Verify

8.1 Expected deliverables

Deliverable Format Verification
Real ownership integration Open-source code Valid and stale ownership tests
Warranty MVP Hosted application Complete Alice → Bob lifecycle
Provider workflows Source code and test reports Provider A/B verification and service usage
Safety regression coverage Automated CI tests Failure and duplicate-request tests
Testnet evidence JSON, transaction hashes, logs Independent public-chain inspection
Early user evaluation Public report Actual participation and feedback summary
Final documentation Markdown and walkthrough Clean-checkout verification

8.2 Independent verification

A reviewer should be able to inspect the result without trusting screenshots or developer assertions alone.

The final evidence package will include:

  • The exact source revision used for testing.

  • Capability Type Script deployment identity and code hash.

  • Testnet issuance and transfer transaction hashes.

  • Input and successor OutPoints.

  • Relevant transaction confirmation evidence.

  • Provider authorization decisions before and after transfer.

  • Care service-event records and remaining-unit transitions.

  • Automated test results.

  • The pilot report and reproduction instructions.

The reviewer can follow these steps:

  1. Open the public SkillPass Care application and follow the guided scenario.

  2. Inspect the published CKB transaction hashes and confirm the ownership transition.

  3. Check that the previous entitlement OutPoint is spent and the successor Cell corresponds to the new holder.

  4. Verify that the post-transfer authorization evidence rejects Alice and accepts Bob.

  5. Inspect the Care service-event report to confirm that two services were recorded and one coverage unit remains.

  6. Review the published CI results for duplicate requests, stale ownership, and unavailable RPC data.

For source-level reproduction, the existing repository provides:

npm install --no-audit --no-fund
npm run check
npm run verify:care

The final release will document any additional configuration and verification commands needed for the integrated Testnet workflow.

Read-only review of published evidence will not require a funded wallet. Repeating the complete live transaction workflow will require a CKB Testnet wallet, Testnet CKB, and RPC connectivity.

Successful completion means a reviewer can verify both the ownership transfer on CKB and the corresponding service-coverage continuity in SkillPass Care.

The project will not substitute synthetic transactions for the required final Testnet evidence.

9. Current State vs. Funded Work

9.1 Work already completed

The existing SkillPass project includes:

  • A Capability Cell model for transferable service entitlements.

  • A CKB Type Script and associated contract tests.

  • Issuance and ownership-transfer logic.

  • Current-owner and stale-owner verification.

  • Wallet connectivity and a hosted interface.

  • A previously completed real CKB Pudge Testnet lifecycle.

A successful GitHub Actions run is publicly available:

github.com

Add files via upload

Real CKB Testnet — Deploy + Lifecycle #6

The previously published Testnet evidence includes:

Contract deployment

0xb340d171bb9cc0e25e580c406bf2379d8753cddfb38920eade177c896e12a39d

Capability issuance

0xbeab784808e46377466605f79be2ea3a0fdeef16e83532d18f735c927025aa25

Alice → Bob transfer

0x223ba748f9bb09c4951e8b0db92f119d1bd046a80d62ece3e33e488d00aafc53

The CKBuilder update reports successful ownership checks by two provider configurations before and after the transfer, including 16 on-chain verification checks.

This is existing protocol evidence, not a completed end-to-end SkillPass Care product pilot.

SkillPass Care already includes:

  • Product-service coverage plans.

  • Remaining-unit accounting.

  • Service-event history.

  • Provider-specific workflow rules.

  • A PostgreSQL-backed application state model.

  • A canonical ownership integration interface.

  • In-memory and persistence-based tests.

  • A hosted product demonstration.

These components are already implemented and are not being submitted as new funded deliverables.

9.2 New work requested from Spark

The requested grant is limited to:

  1. Completing and validating the real canonical Testnet ownership integration within SkillPass Care.

  2. Demonstrating the complete warranty workflow with real ownership transfer and persistent Care state.

  3. Improving the customer/provider experience sufficiently for controlled external testing.

  4. Running an initial product evaluation with potential users and service providers.

  5. Publishing a reproducible technical and usability evidence package.

The distinction is intentional: the existing SkillPass lifecycle establishes that ownership transfer works; the funded pilot will examine whether that capability produces a usable warranty application.

9.3 Scope exclusions

The four-week pilot does not include:

  • Mainnet deployment or handling real customer funds.

  • A new CKB Type Script protocol.

  • A warranty marketplace or payment-processing system.

  • Fiber or x402 integration.

  • DID, reputation, or credential infrastructure.

  • Verification of physical-product possession or legal title.

  • Claims of independent legal or smart-contract security certification.

These exclusions keep the project focused on one measurable product experiment.

10. CKB Alignment and Ecosystem Value

SkillPass Care uses CKB’s Cell model as the ownership foundation for portable service entitlements.

Its main CKB-specific properties are:

Transferable entitlement ownership

A Capability Cell can move between wallet-controlled locks through a CKB transaction. The application derives the current holder from canonical chain state rather than relying on a manually synchronized owner field.

Independent provider authorization

Different providers can verify the same entitlement identity and its current owner without sharing an entitlement-owner database. Each provider can still maintain its own service policies.

Separation of ownership and application state

CKB records the transferable entitlement, while SkillPass Care manages service quotas, history, and provider operations. This avoids putting every repair or diagnostic event on-chain.

Wallet-based control

Customers can use supported CKB wallet mechanisms to control entitlement transfers and prove authorization without giving a warranty provider custody of their private keys.

The experiment aims to determine whether this design is useful for a tangible consumer-facing scenario: transferring remaining service coverage when a second-hand product changes hands.

A successful pilot would provide an open-source example of how a CKB-native service right can support an application used by more than one provider.

An unsuccessful or inconclusive pilot would also provide useful evidence about adoption barriers, wallet friction, operational complexity, or cases where an ordinary database-backed solution is more practical.

11. Risks, Evaluation, and Reporting

Risk Mitigation
Real ownership integration is incomplete Use the existing deployment-pinned SkillPass interfaces and keep unresolved verification fail-closed
Chain or RPC data is unavailable Report an inconclusive state instead of authorizing service
Duplicate or concurrent requests consume excess coverage Apply idempotency and transactional quota checks
Pilot participants are difficult to recruit Begin outreach early and publish actual responses, including unsuccessful outreach
Users find wallet-based warranties too complicated Measure completion difficulties and compare with simpler alternatives
Project scope exceeds four weeks Keep one product scenario, one coverage plan, and two provider configurations

Progress will be reported at the end of each milestone through the repository and Nervos Talk.

The final report will distinguish completed functionality, verified on-chain evidence, external feedback, and any unmet objectives.

12. Expected Outcome

At the end of the four-week Spark pilot, SkillPass Care should provide:

  1. A usable CKB Testnet warranty application demonstrating ownership transfer between two customers.

  2. A complete service lifecycle preserving remaining coverage across that transfer.

  3. Provider workflows that verify the current entitlement holder and reject stale authorization.

  4. Public, reproducible evidence connecting CKB ownership changes with application service records.

  5. Initial feedback establishing whether the product concept is useful and what would be required for a larger pilot.

The requested $500 will support this focused product-validation milestone, not another general-purpose infrastructure layer.

If the pilot establishes meaningful developer or provider interest, a larger deployment or commercial integration can be considered separately.

The immediate goal is more modest: demonstrate one complete application, allow others to verify it, and learn whether transferable warranty coverage is a useful CKB product.

Thank you to the Spark Program Committee and CKBuilder mentors for reviewing the project and supporting its technical development.

I welcome feedback on the proposed scope, acceptance criteria, and whether this focused product pilot is appropriate for Spark funding.

item.title: Spark Program | EasyO: Non-Custodial Pay-to-QR Bridge on CKB
item.dc:creator: Owais
item.description:
Team / Individual Profile

  • Applicant: Owais (GitHub: owaisdotcom) · Full Stack Software Engineer
  • Requested: $2,000 USD, paid 100% in CKB
  • Duration: 8 weeks, 4 milestones · License: MIT
  • Contact: Nervos Talk

1. Overview

EasyO is a non-custodial crypto-to-fiat QR payment bridge that lets users spend Nervos CKB stablecoins (xUDT assets) directly at everyday physical merchants across 10 emerging markets, including India (UPI), Brazil (PIX), Indonesia (QRIS), Vietnam (VietQR), Thailand (PromptPay), and the Philippines (QR Ph).

It enables users to pay through existing merchant QR codes directly from a CKB wallet, while merchants receive settlement in their local fiat currency. No crypto onboarding, POS hardware, or banking changes are required for merchants.

Scope of this Spark grant: The 10-market network is the long-term goal. This grant funds the initial step: a working testnet proof of concept for one corridor (PIX / QRIS), including asset-agnostic CKB escrow scripts, a CCC transaction library, and a live end-to-end demo. The security review, mainnet pilot, open-source SDK, and expansion to additional markets will follow in later proposals.

2. Problem

People in emerging markets who hold stablecoins can’t easily spend them at local coffee shops, grocery stores, or street vendors.

Existing options are mostly custodial apps that require users to trust a third party, or on-chain payment systems that merchants are reluctant to accept because they need immediate settlement in local currency. Local QR payment systems (UPI, PIX, QRIS, PromptPay, QR Ph, and others) are already ubiquitous. What’s missing is a non-custodial way to convert stablecoin balances into local QR payments without users giving up control of their keys.

3. How It Works

1. Scan and On-Chain Escrow: Instead of cashing out through a centralized exchange to a bank account, a user scans a merchant’s existing local payment QR code and signs a single CKB transaction (via JoyID passkey or any CCC-compatible wallet) that locks their stablecoin (xUDT) into an escrow script on CKB.

2. Peer-to-Peer Settlement and Liquidity: Independent local liquidity providers (“fillers”) pay the merchant in local fiat currency through the local QR payment rail, then submit proof of settlement to claim the locked stablecoins on-chain. EasyO does not custody user funds or directly handle fiat, reducing the need for EasyO itself to act as an intermediary in fiat settlement.

3. Built on Proven Volume and Open Infrastructure: Inspired by peer-to-peer QR settlement architectures such as p2p. me / zkp2p on Base, which have processed $31.4M+ in volume across 341,200+ orders, and AnyQR on Cardano. This Spark grant funds the porting of the non-custodial escrow architecture to Nervos CKB as a working testnet proof of concept for one corridor. Integrating existing liquidity networks and releasing an open-source TypeScript/CCC SDK so third-party CKB wallets can embed pay-to-QR functionality natively are planned next steps.

4. Why CKB

  • Transparent escrow. Release, claim, and refund rules live in lock and type scripts that anyone can inspect, allowing users to verify the conditions under which their funds can be released.
  • Payments for people who’ve never used a wallet. JoyID passkeys turn transaction signing into a fingerprint or face scan.
  • Asset-agnostic by design. Stablecoins are represented as xUDT assets on CKB, and the escrow takes the asset’s type script as a parameter. The PoC runs on a testnet xUDT.
  • Reusable infrastructure. The scripts and CCC library will be open source, allowing any CKB wallet or application to integrate pay-to-QR functionality.
  • Real-world utility for CKB stablecoins. Everyday payment use cases create demand beyond simply holding these assets.

5. How the PoC Works

  1. The user scans a PIX / QRIS QR code. The app parses the payload (merchant and fiat amount) and displays the equivalent stablecoin amount using a quoted exchange rate.
  2. The user signs a single CKB transaction locking the stablecoin in an escrow cell, bound to the payment details, claim conditions, and an expiry.
  3. A liquidity provider pays the merchant through the local payment rail.
  4. The provider submits proof of payment and claims the escrow.
  5. If no provider claims before expiry, the user can reclaim the funds without any third-party action.

Proof of settlement and its limitations. For this PoC, claim authorization relies on a provider-signed payment receipt confirmed by the user, followed by a dispute window before the escrow is released. Trust-minimized verification, such as cryptographic proof of fiat payment as implemented in zkp2p, is outside the scope of this proposal and will be explored in a later phase.

6. Deliverables

  1. Escrow lock script (Rust / appropriate framework): Create, claim, and refund paths, parameterized by asset type script, deployed on CKB testnet, with unit tests and published source code.
  2. CCC-based TypeScript library: PIX / QRIS QR payload parsing and lock / claim / refund transaction builders.
  3. Live testnet demo: A minimal web page where a user scans or pastes a QR code, signs with JoyID, and executes the full lifecycle (lock → claim → release, and expiry → refund) end to end, accompanied by a short screen recording.
  4. Design note (in the repository): Script design, trust model, failure cases, and a threat list, including requirements for a mainnet version.
  5. Stablecoin assessment: A comparison of candidate mainnet assets (issuer, liquidity, fiat off-ramp access, and risks), informed by input from the Spark committee and Fiber team.

7. Timeline and Funding

Requested: $2,000 USD equivalent, paid in CKB at the market rate on each disbursement date and released upon verified delivery of each phase. I’m happy to adjust the payment currency to match the committee’s available options.

| Phase | Weeks | Work | Share |

| :— | :— | :— | :— |

| **A** | 1–2 | Escrow design, QR parser, repository setup, stablecoin consultation | $400 (20%) |

| **B** | 3–5 | Script implementation and tests, CCC library, testnet deployment | $700 (35%) |

| **C** | 6–7 | Demo page, lifecycle recording, design note, stablecoin assessment | $700 (35%) |

| **D** | 8 | Documentation and public write-up | $200 (10%) |

| **Total** | | | **$2,000** |

To-do list

  • Confirm the recommended mainnet stablecoin with the Spark committee and Fiber team, and document the decision.
  • Specify escrow cell data layout and script arguments.
  • Implement and test create / claim / refund paths.
  • Parameterize the script by asset and test with at least two different xUDTs on testnet.
  • Implement PIX / QRIS corridor QR parsing with test vectors.
  • Build CCC and JoyID transaction helpers.
  • Deploy on testnet and record the demo.
  • Publish the design note, stablecoin assessment, and README.

8. Success Criteria (Verifiable by the Committee)

  • Escrow scripts deployed on testnet with a public repository and passing tests.
  • The full lifecycle (lock, claim, refund) reproducible from the README.
  • A working JoyID-signed testnet payment demonstrated in the recording.
  • The escrow demonstrated with two different test assets, showing that no asset is hardcoded.
  • A design note documenting the trust assumptions and limitations, alongside a written stablecoin assessment.

9. After Spark

Upon successful delivery, I plan to submit a Community Fund DAO proposal covering an independent security review, a mainnet pilot with real merchants and liquidity providers in the chosen first corridor, an open-source SDK, and expansion into additional markets. I’ll report results publicly at each stage.

10. Risks and Limits

  • Stablecoin availability and off-ramp liquidity Stablecoin options on CKB are evolving, and fiat off-ramps for CKB-native assets are limited. A provider paid in a stablecoin without an accessible off-ramp must convert it before recovering fiat. Mitigation: The escrow is asset-agnostic, allowing the asset to change without redesigning the scripts. The stablecoin assessment is a deliverable. .
  • Proof of settlement. The PoC method described in Section 5 is simplified and not trust-minimized. It should be treated as design validation, not a production-ready settlement mechanism.

11. Value to the Ecosystem

EasyO aims to turn CKB stablecoins (xUDT) from assets primarily held or transferred into assets people can actually spend at everyday merchants in emerging markets, without requiring merchants to handle crypto or users to surrender custody of their funds.

Concrete ecosystem benefits

  • Real-world utility for CKB assets: Creates a practical spending use case for CKB-native stablecoins through existing local QR payment networks such as PIX and QRIS, with a path toward UPI, PromptPay, QR Ph, and other markets. This gives users a reason to hold and use CKB assets beyond transfers and trading.
  • Reusable open infrastructure: The asset-agnostic escrow scripts and CCC/TypeScript library will be MIT-licensed. Any CKB wallet, dApp, or future payment application can reuse the core functionality instead of rebuilding escrow and transaction logic from scratch.
  • Showcasing CKB’s core strengths: Demonstrates how CKB’s Cell Model, programmable scripts, xUDT assets, and JoyID passkeys can work together to deliver a practical, non-custodial payment experience with a familiar QR-based interface.
  • A foundation for liquidity providers: Establishes an architecture through which independent providers can connect CKB stablecoins with existing local payment networks, creating opportunities for third parties to participate without relying on EasyO as the sole settlement intermediary.
  • De-Risking path to mainnet adoption: the ecosystem gets tested open-source primitives, a documented threat model, and a realistic stablecoin off-ramp assessment—giving the Community Fund DAO concrete technical validation before funding an audit or mainnet pilot.
  • Public knowledge and ecosystem visibility: Open-source code, implementation documentation, test vectors, and a recorded end-to-end demonstration give other Nervos developers practical material to learn from, build upon, and integrate into their own projects.

In short, this spark project builds the first open, non-custodial building block that turns CKB stablecoins into everyday payment instruments in the markets where local QR systems already dominate.

item.title: Turnmark: short-round Up/Down prediction markets on CKB, live on testnet
item.dc:creator: Adokiye_Destiny
item.description:
Turnmark lets you take a position on a simple question: will an asset’s price finish higher or lower over a fixed round?

We have BTC/USDT rounds running on Nervos testnet at two durations: 5 minutes and 15 minutes. You deposit test CKB into UP or DOWN before participation closes. The round compares committee-signed prices at its exact start and end boundaries. Winning shares can then be redeemed from the pool.

There is no order book and no house quoting odds. Participants on the two sides fund a shared pot. Your potential payout depends on how much is deposited on each side.

This is a working testnet application, not a mainnet launch. We are sharing it for people to try, review and help shape.

Try it: turnmark.astromind.cc — served over HTTPS.

Source: GitHub repository calledAdo/turnmark.

Addresses and repository paths are written as code here to avoid automatic links.

1. What a round looks like

Suppose a BTC/USDT round runs from 12:00 to 12:05:

  1. Before participation closes, choose UP or DOWN and deposit test CKB. You receive shares tied to that specific pool and side.
  2. Participation is sealed before 12:00. This gives the seal transaction time to confirm before the starting price becomes known.
  3. The exact signed 12:00 SPOT update supplies the starting price, provided the pool also has valid evidence that participation was frozen beforehand.
  4. The exact signed 12:05 SPOT update supplies the ending price.
  5. A higher ending price makes UP the winner. A lower price makes DOWN the winner. An exact tie makes stakes refundable.

The five-minute duration describes the price interval. It does not mean deposits stay open until 12:00, or that payouts are ready exactly at 12:05. Oracle availability, transaction submission and CKB confirmation are separate steps.

You can withdraw while the pool remains OPEN. Once it is sealed, participation is fixed.

How payouts work

This is a parimutuel market: winners recover their stake and share the losing side’s pot, after the configured fee on that losing pot.

For example, with 10 CKB on UP and 10 CKB on DOWN, a 2% fee, and an UP result:

  • The losing pot contributes 9.8 CKB after the 0.2 CKB fee.
  • UP holders share 19.8 CKB in proportion to their winning shares.
  • A participant holding 1 CKB of the 10 CKB UP stake receives 1.98 CKB, before their transaction costs.

The displayed payout is an estimate while deposits and withdrawals can still change the pot. It is not a fixed return. A losing position loses its stake.

2. What lives on CKB

The protocol uses CKB cells and four contracts:

Piece Responsibility
pool_type Validates pool state transitions, boundary-price evidence, accounting and settlement.
pool_admin_lock Separates lifecycle authority from creation and teardown authority.
share_xudt Represents pool-specific UP and DOWN shares and constrains minting and burning.
treasury_lock Guards the treasury used by the xUDT-backed pool path.

The public application currently uses CKB-backed pools. An xUDT path exists in the code, but the funded public-testnet acceptance described below does not establish that path’s readiness.

The core pool lifecycle is:

OPEN
  Deposits and withdrawals allowed
  |
  | SEAL participation before the start boundary
  v
SEALED
  Participation frozen
  |
  | ACTIVATE with exact start price + freeze proof
  v
LOCKED
  Round running
  |
  | RESOLVE with exact end price
  v
FINALIZED
  Winning shares redeemable

Cancellation paths:
  OPEN   -> VOID if empty or one-sided at seal, or on timeout
  SEALED -> VOID on activation timeout
  LOCKED -> VOID on resolution timeout

VOID: stakes refundable
Exact tie: refund outcome

An exact tie follows the refund outcome. After the claim grace period, an authorized maintenance transaction can consume the terminal PoolCell.

3. Why sealing and starting are separate

This is one of the most important parts of the design.

If deposits and the starting price were fixed in one transaction submitted at the boundary, that transaction might confirm after the price was already known. Participation could remain open too late.

Turnmark separates those events:

  • SEAL freezes participation ahead of the boundary.
  • ACTIVATE records the exact boundary price and verifies a signed checkpoint covering the actual sealed cell’s origin.

The checkpoint binds the network, boundary and accepted chain history. The contract checks the sealed cell’s origin and its header ancestry against that certificate.

There is an explicit trust limit: the committee attests to its external observation time and accepted chain cut. CKB headers alone cannot prove that something happened before a real-world wall-clock deadline.

Without acceptable freeze evidence, the pool must not start. The timeout path allows cancellation and refunds instead.

4. Where the prices come from

Turnmark uses Lean Oracle, introduced in the Nervos Talk post “Asset price oracle on Nervos Network” (topic 10800, at talk.nervos.org/t/asset-price-oracle-on-nervos-network/10800). That post explains the oracle’s publishers, signed updates and public mirror; this post focuses on how Turnmark uses them for prediction rounds.

Turnmark consumes the oracle through lean-oracle-sdk. Oracle publishers, price production and the public mirror run independently of this project’s workers.

For settlement, the pool pins its feed, exponent and publisher committee. ACTIVATE and RESOLVE verify the signed update directly, including quorum signatures and the feed’s Merkle inclusion proof. The live publisher-set cell is referenced as a read-only cell dependency.

The current product uses boundary SPOT, not TWAP:

  • Start price: the signed update whose timestamp exactly equals the configured start boundary.
  • End price: the signed update whose timestamp exactly equals the configured close boundary.
  • A later price is not substituted simply because the required update is unavailable.

The browser’s live chart is informational. It is not settlement evidence. The contract verifies the signed boundary update supplied in the transaction.

This also means oracle methodology matters. An exact signed SPOT tick proves what the committee signed; it does not make instantaneous markets immune to manipulation or guarantee a price will always be available.

5. What the backend does—and what it cannot do

Workers keep rounds moving. They create pools, seal participation, obtain boundary proofs, submit activation and resolution transactions, handle timeout cancellations and eventually clean up terminal pools.

Each asset-duration pair is a separate lane. BTC/USDT 5m and BTC/USDT 15m have their own schedules and worker services.

Within each lane, wallet responsibilities are split:

Rail Actions
Lifecycle SEAL, ACTIVATE, RESOLVE and timeout VOID
Maintenance CREATE and CLOSE

This keeps low-priority creation and teardown transactions from occupying the same wallet resources as boundary work. Different pools and lanes can progress concurrently, while actions spending the same PoolCell must serialize.

A shared database records lanes, pools, durable jobs, transaction attempts and resource leases. Workers revalidate chain state before spending. The indexer reconciles confirmations and exposes read APIs to the frontend.

Before broadcast, the executor persists the transaction hash and exact signed bytes. If submission returns an ambiguous response, it retains the reservation and reconciles that same transaction rather than assuming failure and building a conflicting replacement.

These mechanisms help recovery, but do not make the infrastructure fully independent: lanes still share the host, database, indexer and external services.

The backend does not choose a winning side by writing a result into its database. Settlement must satisfy the on-chain rules. However, operators still have availability responsibilities and control authorized sealing, timeout cancellation and teardown. This is not an operator-free system.

6. Using the application

Open turnmark.astromind.cc, connect a supported wallet and use its displayed CKB receiving address to fund it with testnet CKB.

The application includes:

  • A market view with the live indicative chart and entry ticket.
  • Positions, with active holdings and available claims or refunds.
  • Results for completed rounds.
  • A wallet panel with the CKB address, balance and CKB transfer flow.
  • A shared transaction tracker for signing, submission, confirmation and failure.

EVM wallets such as MetaMask connect through CCC. The wallet panel exposes the corresponding CKB address; the application still transacts on CKB testnet.

Some activity history is browser-local, rather than a complete account-wide historical index. Changing browser or origin does not carry that local history across.

7. What we have actually tested

On 13 November, we completed a funded public-testnet acceptance run covering one real 5-minute pool and one real 15-minute pool.

Each pool received one 1 CKB UP deposit and one 1 CKB DOWN deposit. Both finalized with UP as the winner. Winner redemptions and losing-share burns were confirmed, with each winner receiving the expected 1.98 CKB.

A separate read-only chain verification script checked:

  • All eight participant transactions, including exact signed bytes and witnesses.
  • The four exact start/end price proofs.
  • The consumed sealed cells and their ancestry to the signed checkpoints.
  • Payouts and zero remaining participant shares.

This was our own acceptance verification, not an external security audit.

The report is in docs/testnet-freeze-rails-acceptance-2026-11-13.md, with public evidence under docs/evidence/testnet-freeze-rails-2026-11-13/.

These two rounds demonstrate an end-to-end flow, not a reliability guarantee. Boundary submissions were acknowledged roughly 2.8–4.2 seconds after their boundaries; observed confirmations were roughly 20–62 seconds after them. Those measurements include different stages and should not be described as instant settlement.

8. Current limits

Testnet only. This is not a claim of mainnet readiness. Use faucet CKB.

One live oracle publisher. The current committee is 1-of-1. Threshold verification exists, but multiple independent operators are not yet providing the live trust model.

Larger committees need further work. The combined activation verifier measured about 112 million cycles at 7-of-9, exceeding the default 70-million-cycle transaction-pool verification limit. We cannot claim that increasing the committee is already a deployment-only change.

Claims have a finite window. Terminal pools can be torn down after a grace period measured from the scheduled close: eight times the round duration, bounded between one hour and seven days. That is one hour for 5m rounds and two hours for 15m rounds. Do not assume winnings or refunds remain claimable indefinitely. This policy deserves review before mainnet.

Refunds require transactions. A VOID outcome makes principal redeemable; it does not automatically send it back to every wallet. Transaction fees and capacity requirements still apply.

Infrastructure can delay progress. Oracle or RPC outages, shared-host failures and CKB confirmations affect availability. Separate wallet rails reduce one source of contention; they do not eliminate those dependencies.

More acceptance gates remain. Larger-quorum admission, xUDT pools, governance rotation, broader crash/contention testing and longer operational soak are still separate work.

9. What feedback would help

We would appreciate people trying a full testnet flow: connect, deposit, follow a round, then claim a win or refund. Tell us where the interface makes the rules or transaction status unclear.

For contract and protocol reviewers, we especially want scrutiny of:

  • Participation freezing and checkpoint trust assumptions.
  • Exact-boundary SPOT settlement and missing-price behavior.
  • Share accounting, payouts and refunds.
  • Operator authority, timeout behavior and claim-window policy.
  • Transaction recovery and conflicting-cell handling.

For product feedback: are 5m and 15m useful durations? Is the early deposit cutoff understandable? What would you need to see before trusting a market like this?

I will answer questions and share progress in this thread.

item.title: Community Fund DAO voting in numbers
item.dc:creator: LusoCryptoLabs
item.description:
Since 2023, 178 people have voted in the Community Fund DAO, about 1% of the 16,610 Nervos DAO depositors. We wanted to understand why more holders do not take part, and found one reason that can be fixed: 1,132 depositors can only vote if they move their deposit to Neuron first, because the wallet they use cannot bind today. Other reasons need asking, so there is a short poll at the end.

Read from CKB mainnet at block 21,038,015 and from Metaforo’s public API, both on 2026-11-17, read only. We build Ward and the Cellula wallet and had a proposal in this DAO (t/11089, passed on 16 November), so we waited for its vote to close before posting this. The scripts and raw data are available to anyone who wants to check them.

How a vote is counted today

Metaforo binds a CKB address with a message signed the way Neuron signs (secp256k1), which is how most people held CKB when the DAO started. A vote weighs the Nervos DAO deposits under the bound addresses. All 614 addresses bound by the 178 people who have ever voted are secp256k1 addresses. Logging in with JoyID works, but deposits under the JoyID address are not counted.

1. Who votes

39 votes since February 2023. The median vote had 15 voters and 1.2% of the DAO’s deposits on its closing day (94.0M CKB; 155.0M over the last 12 months). The highest were 50 voters (Rosen Bridge integration, January 2026) and 7.3% of deposits (Community Fund DAO v1.1, November 2025).

178 people have ever voted, 81 of them in the last 12 months. The addresses voters bound hold 980.0M CKB in deposits today, 12.0% of the DAO.

2. Who cannot vote from their own wallet

Live Nervos DAO deposits: 8,179,234,336 CKB under 16,610 locks (the explorer shows the same two numbers). By the lock that holds them:

Lock Depositors CKB in deposits Share
secp256k1 (Neuron and most wallets) 15,478 7,789,223,487 95.23%
JoyID 120 171,535,773 2.10%
PW-lock (Portal Wallet) 926 159,203,037 1.95%
Omnilock, Ethereum mode (MetaMask through CCC) 78 39,562,830 0.48%
Quantum-resistant lock (Quantum Purse) 5 15,310,092 0.19%
iCKB pool 1 2,857,481 0.03%
Omnilock, Bitcoin mode (UniSat, OKX through CCC) 1 1,483,000 0.02%
other 1 58,636 0.00%

Deposits outside secp256k1 cannot be bound today: 1,132 depositors with 390.0M CKB (4.8%). Portal Wallet had a path in 2023 (t/7053), but none of the 614 bound addresses is a PW-lock. Leaving PW-lock aside, it is 206 depositors with 230.8M CKB (2.8%). Some voters already log in with JoyID; deposits under their JoyID addresses are not counted today.

These wallets use the DAO more than most: JoyID holders keep 37% of their CKB in deposits, PW-lock 56%, Omnilock 31%, the quantum-resistant lock 49%. For secp256k1 addresses it is about 16% (approximate, see the limits).

The wallet is not the main reason people do not vote: about 15,000 depositors can bind today and have not. Why, the chain cannot say.

3. The 30 day lock

Weight needs the CKB in the DAO, and leaving it takes up to about 30 days. How many holders stay out for that reason, the chain cannot tell either: most of the CKB outside the DAO (about 41.7B) sits with exchanges, team and foundation addresses. 843.2M CKB is in phase 1 of a withdrawal right now.

Counting any wallet

Counting deposits from any lock would let the 1,132 depositors above vote from the wallet they already use. One way is a lock proof, which we have been building as Ward (GitHub - LusoCryptoLabs/ckb-ward: Ward: lock proof for CKB. Prove control of any CKB lock with a proof transaction that can never land on chain. · GitHub); votes signed by the deposit’s own lock, as in ckb-treasury-lab, are another. We are happy to help with either.

If you hold CKB and have not voted

What is the main reason?

  • I did not know about these votes
  • My wallet cannot bind (JoyID, MetaMask, UniSat, OKX, other)
  • Binding and voting take too much effort
  • My CKB is on an exchange
  • I do not want it locked in the Nervos DAO
  • My vote would not change the result
  • Other (please reply)

Click to view the poll.

Method and limits

  • Deposits: every live cell with the Nervos DAO type at block 21,038,015 (indexer get_cells); data of 8 zero bytes is a deposit, anything else a withdrawal in progress.
  • Lock kinds from CCC’s list of mainnet scripts; the Omnilock mode from the first byte of its args; the quantum-resistant lock and iCKB identified by code hash.
  • Votes, bound addresses, login keys and each voter’s weight from Metaforo’s public API (39 polls, 178 voter profiles). Shares use the explorer’s daily DAO total on each closing day.
  • A depositor here is a distinct lock. One person can hold several, and an exchange can hold many people’s CKB under one. Large voters are not identified.
  • The total held by secp256k1 addresses is circulating supply less the other lock families, because the public indexer timed out adding up every secp256k1 cell. That makes the 16% approximate.

item.title: What recent mainnet transactions cost in cycles, script by script
item.dc:creator: tun_tunn03
item.description:
I replayed recent CKB mainnet transactions in ckb-debugger, one run per script group, to see where the cycles go. Every transaction is checked against the node: the groups have to add up exactly to the cycles the node recorded for it, or the transaction is listed as excluded instead of counted.

There are two samples, kept apart on purpose.

  1. A random sample: every non-cellbase transaction in every 12th block from 20,932,885 to 20,946,673 (5 Nov 12:54 to 7 Nov 04:00 UTC, about 39 hours). 1,002 transactions, all 1,002 matched the node, nothing excluded.
  Script                              Groups   Median        p90           Share
  secp256k1_blake160 (lock)           1,002    1,647,946     1,665,060     71.9%
  unknown 0xa9267ff5...e981 (type)    175      1,801,237     1,836,377     13.7%
  Type ID (type)                      175      1,000,000     1,000,000     7.6%
  Bitcoin SPV client, RGB++ (type)    33       1,366,700     1,551,628     2.0%
  d.id time oracle, info (type)       648      45,174        45,175        1.3%
  JoyID (lock)                        4        6,833,689     6,862,057     1.2%
  d.id time oracle, index (type)      648      32,977        32,977        0.9%
  4 unknown locks (see below)         175 each 4,426 to 72,371             1.3%
  Nervos DAO (type)                   11       11,981        14,084        <0.01%

Per transaction: median 1,729,190 cycles, p90 4,607,770, max 6,865,540.

  1. A targeted sample. The random window has few or no xUDT, Omnilock or Spore transactions, so for 22 scripts I asked the node’s indexer for the most recent transactions in which each one ran (searching back from block 20,947,093, up to 3,000,000 blocks for the rare ones) and replayed up to 40 of each. 650 replays: 604 matched the node, none mismatched, and 46 older transactions (all at or before block 19,011,137) have no cycle total on the public node, so they are listed as not recorded rather than counted. These were picked by script, so they say what a script costs when it runs, not how much of mainnet it is. No shares here.
  Script (per group)                  Matched groups   Median       p90
  xUDT                                41               20,564       20,717
  Omnilock, Ethereum displaying       37               1,460,165    1,476,761
  Omnilock, Bitcoin                   40               1,458,571    1,472,092
  JoyID                               40               6,815,869    6,879,521
  Spore                               40               105,299      272,482
  Spore Cluster                       40               98,683       122,630
  ckb-dex lock                        39               24,267       39,032
  RGB++ lock                          1,444            1,418,522    1,419,245
  BTC time lock (RGB++)               9                813,924      959,098
  COTA                                49               2,332,001    2,332,001
  iCKB limit order                    40               75,304       79,679
  iCKB logic                          8                105,870      160,850
  anyone-can-pay                      40               34,106       1,609,984
  sUDT                                20               5,540        32,871
  d.id das-lock                       61               282,271      3,862,283
  Nervos DAO                          40               11,974       13,826
  Type ID                             40               1,000,000    1,000,000

What I take from it:

  1. Most of mainnet’s verification cost is still the default lock: secp256k1_blake160 is 71.9% of all cycles in this window, 1.60M to 1.67M per group for 90% of them. It runs once per distinct owner, so a transaction that spends cells of many owners costs that many times more. There was no such transaction in this window (the costliest was 6,865,540 cycles); in a window I measured on 28 Oct, one with 68 owners cost 111,979,599.

  2. 648 of the 1,002 random transactions are d.id’s time oracle updating its timestamp and block number cells. The two type scripts are cheap (about 45k and 33k); the cost of those transactions is the lock.

  3. 175 transactions follow one pattern I cannot name yet: secp256k1_blake160, a Type ID cell, a type script with code hash 0xa9267ff5…e981 at about 1.8M cycles, and four small locks (4,426 to 72,371 cycles). About 4.61M cycles per transaction. Their code cells were deployed in October 2021 and June 2022, so this is not a new protocol. It was in the targeted Type ID sample on 28 Oct as well (26 of 40), but not in that random window.

  4. Type scripts are cheap next to locks. xUDT runs at about 20k cycles, Spore and Cluster around 100k, sUDT under 33k. In an xUDT transfer the lock is most of the bill: the commonest xUDT pattern in the sample was JoyID plus xUDT (16 of 40), at a median of 6,851,229 cycles for the whole transaction, against 1,677,720 for secp256k1 plus xUDT.

  5. Locks vary a lot. Omnilock in Ethereum or Bitcoin mode is about 1.46M, close to secp256k1. JoyID is about 6.8M per group, four times that. The RGB++ lock is about 1.42M per group, but RGB++ transactions spend many cells with distinct args: 36 of the 40 sampled RGB++ transactions ran 40 RGB++ lock groups each and cost about 57M cycles.

  6. Type ID shows exactly 1,000,000 because the node verifies it natively and charges a fixed amount; the tools charge the same.

I made the same measurement on 28 Oct with an older version of the tool. 389 transactions are in both runs (mostly in the targeted samples), and every one gave the same cycles for every group. So the differences between the two reports come from which transactions were on chain in each window, not from the tool.

The full report (min, median, p90 and max for each script, an example transaction, the cell each script’s code was loaded from, what ran together, and every excluded transaction with its reason): ckb-cycle-tools/atlas/2026-11-07/report.md at main · luongthanhtung03/ckb-cycle-tools · GitHub

The raw per-transaction, per-group results are in data.json next to it. The 28 Oct run is still there for comparison: ckb-cycle-tools/atlas/2026-10-28/report.md at main · luongthanhtung03/ckb-cycle-tools · GitHub

How it is measured: ckb-cycle-tools rebuilds each transaction as a ckb-debugger mock transaction from the node (input cells, cell deps with dep groups expanded, header deps) and runs each script group on the CKB-VM version of its block. Script names come from CCC’s known scripts plus a short table of code hashes published elsewhere (Spore and Cluster in @ckb-ccc/spore, RGB++ in rgbpp-sdk, d.id in its own repositories, iCKB’s deployment file, the ckb-dex SDK), each with its source next to it. Scripts with no published hash stay “unknown”. To reproduce the random sample:

  npm ci
  npm run atlas -- --rpc https://mainnet.ckb.dev/ --to 20946673 --blocks 13789 --stride 12 --max-txs 1002

The command for the targeted samples is at the end of the report; --script takes a script name or any code hash, so you can point it at your own script.

The numbers do not depend on the debugger release. 24 recorded transactions (22 mainnet, one for each script sampled above, and 2 testnet) were replayed under 16 ckb-debugger builds, every release from 0.121.0 to 1.1.2 (16 Nov), native and WebAssembly. Every build gave the same cycles for every group: ckb-cycle-tools/compat/RESULTS.md at main · luongthanhtung03/ckb-cycle-tools · GitHub

To measure your own contract before it reaches mainnet: since ckb-cycle-tools 1.1.0 on npm, a project made from ckb-script-templates can use its ckb-testtool tests as the scenarios (ckb-cycles scan, then ckb-cycles report). Steps: GitHub - luongthanhtung03/ckb-cycle-tools · GitHub

Two questions for anyone who knows mainnet traffic better than I do:

  • 24 scripts in these transactions are still unknown to me, among them the 0xa9267ff5…e981 type script and the four locks from point 3. The report shows each one’s code hash (shortened; the full hashes are in data.json) next to the scripts it ran with. If you know one and can point to where its code hash is published, I will name it.
  • Is there a script or a set of transactions you would like measured this way?

This is a snapshot, not a service. The tool is ckb-cycle-tools, MIT: GitHub - luongthanhtung03/ckb-cycle-tools · GitHub

item.title: [DIS] CKB × NEAR Intents: Building a Cross-Chain Bridge and Multichain Swap Gateway
item.dc:creator: asondev
item.description:
[DIS] CKB × NEAR Intents: Building a Cross-Chain Bridge and Multichain Swap Gateway

Funding Requested: 7,000 USDT equivalent
Estimated Duration: 8 weeks
Applicant / Team: FoundationLab
GitHub: ckbswap

1. Executive Summary

This project proposes building a bridge between CKB and NEAR and integrating with NEAR Intents to create a gateway for exchanging CKB across blockchain ecosystems.

Users will be able to bridge CKB to NEAR, receive its bridged representation, nCKB, and exchange it for a target asset through an intent-based swap flow. In the reverse direction, users will be able to exchange supported assets for nCKB and redeem it for native CKB.

The project will cover architecture, bridge contracts, MPC signing, relayer services, Intents integration, a reference quoting service, a user interface, and testing documentation. The deliverable will be a reproducible testnet prototype demonstrating the complete bridge-and-swap lifecycle.

We request 7,000 USDT equivalent from the CKB Community Fund DAO to complete this work over 8 weeks, establishing the technical foundation for future mainnet integration and liquidity partnerships.

2. Background and Motivation

Expanding CKB’s adoption requires making it easier for users from other ecosystems to acquire and use CKB, while giving CKB holders access to a broader range of assets and applications.

A bridge enables asset transfers between networks. An exchange integration addresses the next question: what can users do with those assets after bridging?

This project combines both capabilities:

Native CKB → nCKB on NEAR → NEAR Intents settlement → Target asset

The reverse path will be:

Source asset → NEAR Intents settlement → nCKB → Native CKB redemption

NEAR Intents provides infrastructure for expressing desired outcomes, obtaining quotes, and settling exchanges. Its documentation describes cross-chain swap interfaces and custom contract integrations. NEAR Intents documentation

By connecting CKB to this infrastructure, the project aims to reduce the friction of entering and leaving the CKB ecosystem and make CKB more accessible to multichain users and applications.

3. Project Objectives

Build a bidirectional CKB–NEAR bridge

Implement CKB deposits, nCKB issuance on NEAR, nCKB burning, and withdrawals back to CKB.

nCKB will follow the NEP-141 token standard and use a reserve accounting model designed around 1 nCKB representing 1 CKB. Deposit, issuance, withdrawal, and reserve reconciliation rules will be documented publicly.

Enable intent-based nCKB swaps

Implement the integration needed to deposit nCKB into an Intents settlement contract, query balances, obtain quotes, sign swap intents, execute settlement, and withdraw assets.

This phase will include a reference quoting and execution service that demonstrates bidirectional swaps between nCKB and at least one test asset in a controlled environment.

Provide a unified user interface

Users will be able to view deposit addresses, select a swap direction, review quotes and fees, and track bridge and swap progress through one interface.

Establish a foundation for broader CKB distribution

Publish reusable interfaces and documentation for future integrations with wallets, aggregators, and cross-chain applications.

The initial scope focuses on native CKB. Support for additional CKB ecosystem assets will be evaluated separately based on demand, security requirements, and liquidity availability.

4. Product and Technical Design

CKB-to-NEAR deposits

Users deposit CKB into designated addresses. After the configured number of confirmations, an authorized relayer submits the deposit record to the NEAR bridge contract, which processes nCKB issuance.

Deposits will be identified by transaction hash and output index to prevent duplicate processing and associate each deposit with its recipient and amount.

NEAR-to-CKB withdrawals

Users submit withdrawal requests, and the bridge contract handles nCKB burning and withdrawal state.

The system will use NEAR Chain Signatures to request MPC signatures for CKB withdrawal transactions. The contract will validate recipient amounts and change destinations, while the relayer handles broadcasting, confirmation tracking, and status updates.

NEAR Intents integration

After bridging, nCKB can enter an intent-based exchange flow. A reference execution service will provide quotes and submit compatible execution intents alongside the user’s signed intent.

The testing environment will use the open-source NEAR Intents Verifier contract and test assets to validate actual contract settlement. Project-operated test deployments will be clearly distinguished from production services. NEAR Intents contracts

The project will also prepare asset integration information, quoting interfaces, and liquidity requirements for future production integration.

Public nCKB swaps will require execution providers willing to quote and supply liquidity. Issuing a bridged token does not automatically make it available across the public swap network. NEAR Intents’ asset onboarding guidance identifies liquidity and solver coordination as part of this process. Token onboarding guidance

User interface

A lightweight web application will support:

  • Wallet connection, CKB deposit addresses, and balance viewing.
  • Deposits, swaps, and CKB redemption.
  • Quotes, minimum received amounts, fees, and quote expiry.
  • Deposit confirmation, settlement, and withdrawal tracking.
  • Transaction history and block explorer links.
  • Clear handling of unavailable quotes, expired quotes, and service errors.

5. Value to the CKB Ecosystem

Broader access to CKB. The project will establish a technical route for users from other ecosystems to acquire CKB with fewer manual steps.

More opportunities to use CKB. CKB holders will gain a foundation for accessing other assets and applications through a unified flow, supporting future payment and cross-chain use cases.

New liquidity connections. Intents-based quoting and execution can create opportunities to connect CKB with external market makers and asset networks. Actual depth and pricing will depend on liquidity participation.

Greater ecosystem visibility. Open-source integrations, demonstrations, and developer documentation will introduce CKB to more NEAR and multichain developers and reduce future integration work.

Reusable public infrastructure. The funded work will include bridge contracts, signing adapters, relayers, Intents integration, and a reference interface that other teams can inspect and reuse.

Success will be measured through verifiable software deliverables rather than speculative promises about users, trading volume, or total value locked.

6. Development Plan and Acceptance Criteria

Milestone Timeline Deliverables Acceptance Criteria Amount
M1: Architecture and integration design Weeks 1–2 Bridge architecture, asset flows, permission model, Intents interfaces, and liquidity plan Publish the design, including quoting, settlement, fees, and failure handling 1,000 USDT
M2: Bidirectional bridge Weeks 3–4 nCKB contract, MPC signing adapter, deposit and withdrawal relayers Demonstrate CKB deposits, nCKB issuance, and native CKB redemption on testnet 2,500 USDT
M3: Intents swaps and interface Weeks 5–6 Settlement integration, reference quoting service, and user interface Demonstrate bidirectional swaps between nCKB and at least one test asset, with settlement records 2,000 USDT
M4: Verification and public delivery Weeks 7–8 Failure testing, fixes, documentation, demonstration, and final report At least two accounts complete a combined 10 bridge-and-swap test cycles; publish code, records, and reproduction instructions 1,500 USDT
Total 8 weeks 7,000 USDT

Testing will cover duplicate deposits, unauthorized calls, invalid withdrawal outputs, quote expiry, slippage limits, replay protection, signing failures, and relayer restarts.

A public mainnet swap service requires additional security review, asset onboarding, and production liquidity. Third-party listing or launch commitments are outside this phase’s acceptance criteria.

7. Budget and Disbursement

Budget Item Amount
Bidirectional bridge contracts and deposit/withdrawal relayers 2,500 USDT
NEAR MPC and CKB signing adapter 1,500 USDT
Intents integration and reference quoting service 1,500 USDT
User interface 800 USDT
Testing, documentation, and demonstration 500 USDT
Deployment and operating costs during delivery 200 USDT
Total 7,000 USDT

Disbursement is proposed upon acceptance of each milestone. The budget and milestone tables describe the same funding allocation and are not additive.

The request is denominated in USDT equivalent. The payment asset and conversion method will follow the DAO’s approved arrangement.

This budget covers development and test delivery. It does not include mainnet liquidity capital, trading incentives, a formal third-party security audit, or ongoing production operations.

8. Security and Operational Boundaries

This phase will use authorized relayers to report CKB deposits. The trust assumptions will be disclosed, with permission controls, pause functionality, and processing limits.

MPC provides distributed signing. It does not replace deposit verification, bridge contract security, or administrative controls.

Withdrawal transactions will be checked for recipient, amount, and change destination. Complete on-chain enforcement of miner fees requires trustworthy input information.

Bridging and swapping involve multiple execution steps. Atomic settlement within the Intents contract does not make the entire cross-chain journey atomic. Each stage will have separate tracking and documented recovery procedures.

Swaps will require valid quotes, minimum received amounts, expiry conditions, and replay protection. Unavailable quotes will prevent execution.

A withdrawal that has already received a valid signature cannot be refunded solely because it timed out: the signed transaction might still be broadcast. Recovery procedures must prevent duplicate payouts.

The funded release is a testnet prototype. Mainnet deployment, formal external auditing, light-client or SPV deposit verification, and a complete multi-relayer consensus system are outside this phase.

9. Open Source, Maintenance, and Community Updates

Source code, tests, deployment scripts, and documentation will be published under a clearly specified open-source license, respecting dependency licenses.

Progress updates will be published every two weeks. Final delivery will include:

  • Deployable bridge and Intents integration code.
  • A testnet interface and demonstration video.
  • Deposit, swap, and withdrawal records.
  • A test report, deployment guide, and security documentation.
  • Asset integration materials and production liquidity requirements.

Long-term operations and mainnet maintenance will require a separate ownership and funding arrangement.

10. Funding Request

We request 7,000 USDT equivalent to build a bidirectional CKB–NEAR bridge and demonstrate asset exchange through NEAR Intents.

The goal is to establish a multichain gateway for CKB: making it easier for external users to acquire CKB, enabling CKB holders to access more assets and applications, and expanding CKB’s reach through open, reusable integrations.
